#9774. Your CRM Stage Probabilities Were Made Up - Calibrate Them in an Afternoon

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Open your CRM's opportunity stages and look at the probability next to each one. Discovery 10%. Qualified 20%. Solution 40%. Proposal 60%. Negotiation 80%. Verbal 90%.

Where did those numbers come from? In most companies, nobody knows. They were set when the CRM was implemented, often by copying a template, and they've never been checked. Yet, they drive the weighted pipeline number that shows up in forecast calls and board decks.

Checking them takes an afternoon and one SQL query, as long as you have one thing: a snapshot of the pipeline at a fixed point in time.

For each of the last several quarters, you need the list of deals that were open on the first day of the quarter, with the stage each one was in that day. Most CRMs keep field history, and most warehouses that sync a CRM keep daily snapshots. If you have neither, start saving a snapshot today and come back in two quarters.

The first-day snapshot matters. If you look at deals in their current stage, you'll only see the deals that are still open or the stage they died in, which tells you nothing about how likely a deal was to close when it was at that stage.

Then join each snapshot deal to how it ended: won at any point, and won in the same quarter.

I simulated eight quarters of first-day snapshots, about 3,400 deal-quarters, with the usual 10/20/40/60/80/90 probabilities in the CRM and different true win rates underneath.

The CRM's probabilities are too high even for eventual wins. A deal in Negotiation is won 57% of the time, not 80%. A deal in Solution is won 28% of the time, not 40%. This is common. Stage probabilities are usually set by optimists, and they're rarely lowered.

The forecast needs a different number entirely. A stage probability answers "will this deal ever close?" A quarterly forecast needs "will this deal close this quarter?" Those differ a lot for early stages. A Solution-stage deal on the first day of the quarter has a 28% chance of eventually closing, but only a 14% chance of closing before the quarter ends. Early-stage deals take time.

The last column weights by deal value. If it differs a lot from the deal count version, big deals behave differently from small ones, and you should calibrate by size band too.

The real test is whether the measured rates forecast better than the CRM's. I learned the rates from the first four quarters and tested them on the last four, which is the honest way to check. Testing on the same quarters you learned from will always look good.

The CRM-weighted pipeline says about $4.6 million every quarter. About $2 million actually closes. The CRM number is more than twice the truth. The measured rates come in about 10% low, close enough to be useful, and the error is consistent enough that you could see it and adjust after a quarter or two.

A weighted pipeline that's off by more than 2x isn't just inaccurate. It's actively harmful, because people make hiring and spending decisions based on it.

Stage skipping. If reps often jump deals straight to Proposal, the deals in Proposal on the first day are a mix of real proposals and deals that never had discovery. That's fine for calibration. You're measuring what Proposal means in practice, not in the sales playbook.

Re-opened and recycled deals. If lost deals get re-opened later, decide whether a re-open is the same deal or a new one, and be consistent.

Changing processes. If the stage definitions changed a year ago, only use quarters after the change. Fewer quarters of the right data beat more quarters of the wrong data.

Small numbers. With 94 deals in Verbal across eight quarters, the 84% is reasonably solid. If a stage has 20 deals, the measured rate could easily be off by 15 points. Pool more quarters, or merge thin stages.

Update the CRM probabilities to the eventual win rates. They're used in lots of places, and the eventual rate is what the field implies.

Use the same-quarter rates for the quarterly forecast. Keep them in a small table in the warehouse, not in the CRM, and recompute them every quarter from the latest eight quarters.

Show both numbers in the forecast meeting. "Weighted pipeline at the CRM's probabilities is $4.6 million. At measured rates, it's $1.8 million." The first time the meeting sees that, the conversation changes.

Recalibrate on a schedule. Win rates drift as products, markets, and teams change. Put a calendar reminder at the start of each quarter.

None of this needs a forecasting tool. It needs a pipeline snapshot, one query, and the willingness to replace a number everybody's used to with one that's right.

I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about pipeline, forecasting, and the numbers behind them at malekdamiri.com.

#9773. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

This entry was posted on Friday 20th of November 2026 07:36 PM

i don’t get it. the client shouts ‘i refuse to pay these buzzards one cent!’ fine, we’ll deal with it. we won’t pay the ransom. but you know how much they demanded and we’re going to ask you to pay 20% more. it will cost you more but, heck, you’re doing the right thing. don’t pay those buzzards. and that is fraud. but were the ‘bad guys’ simply to tell the client ‘heck, it’s a shame. but there’s no other way out. you can pay one of my prominent competitors, and they’ll tell you the only thing you can do is negotiate with the bad guys. fix up the system next time. so the only difference between the fraudster and the ‘highly regarded’ intermediary is that the former doesn’t bother to convince the client there is no choice. this escobar fellow from medellin [really?] should have negotiated a discount, taken a cut off the top, and called it a day like the legitimate dudes. oh wait. that’s exactly what he did try to do…

The marketing copy is the tell here: a company claiming 100% recovery with proprietary cryptographic tools was doing neither, because real decryption is either possible with the attacker’s key or it is not – there is no proprietary middle ground that beats the mathematics. The markup model also poisoned the incident response itself: victims who paid a negotiator instead of the attacker directly had no idea the same group was on both sides of the transaction. Worth noting the 404 Media report apparently missed the company name; the indictment PDF is the primary source worth reading.

it would seem that any intermediary negotiating on behalf of a client in the dark web is operating on both sides of the transaction. i guess that was my point.

Probably one of the most common is that there are other soon-to-be defendants that are in the orbit of the accused but not yet charged or arrested, and the government would rather not make their own job harder.

And who happens to be listed as a board member of ransomwarehelp, no other than Don Jr. The grifting never ends…

#9772. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

#9770. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9768. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9767. Fledge Launches World Connection Day on November 21 to Fight Loneliness

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

New York, United States, November 20th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--Fledge, a dating app built on psychological compatibility, is launching World Connection Day (WCD) on November 21, 2026, a worldwide initiative encouraging people in cities across the US, Canada and Europe to meet new people in local squares, parks and waterfronts. The initiative aims to encourage social connection and address loneliness through simple, face-to-face interactions. Participation is free and does not require registration.

On Saturday, November 21, 2026, people will head to local squares, parks and waterfronts wearing a colored ribbon on their wrist. There are four ribbon colors, and each participant receives theirs after a short, playful hello-style test.

The color reflects how the person approaches a conversation and how ready they are to start one. Whatever the color, the ribbon means one thing - you can say hello to me. World Connection Day (WCD) is a worldwide day for meeting new people, started by Fledge, a dating app based on psychological compatibility.

The idea comes from the same place as the app: the better you understand yourself, the easier it is to recognize who is right for you. Fledge puts psychological compatibility at the core of its product, matching people by how they think, communicate and connect rather than by photos alone. WCD brings that approach offline and the test shows people their own style of saying hello and which style pairs best with it, so the first step toward a stranger feels less like a gamble.

Loneliness is no longer a niche topic. The World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection reports that 1 in 6 people worldwide experience loneliness, with loneliness linked to more than 871,000 deaths annually. The WHO also identifies loneliness and social isolation as factors that increase the risk of serious health problems, including cardiovascular disease, depression and anxiety. But loneliness also shapes everyday life.

When something wonderful happens and there’s no one to call, small moments like that add up to a bigger question of whether you have people you can count on. Being single doesn’t automatically mean being lonely, because friends, family and community can all provide closeness. What matters is having relationships in which you feel known and accepted.

"Having spent years developing the dating app to bring people together, I know the main obstacle isn't discovering a match—it's breaking the ice," said Val Klimov, the founder of Fledge, whose platforms have reached 20 million users. "The ribbon removes that hesitation. Wearing it signals that you welcome a conversation. During initial testing at Web Summit, 35% of attendees selected red for the bold hello, while 30% picked blue for the deep hello. Courage takes different forms. Certain individuals take the lead, whereas others prefer a thoughtful prompt. Ultimately, no one wants to take that step alone."

Every ribbon means the same thing: you can say hello to me. No color is a warning, so red isn’t “stop” and yellow isn’t “busy.” A ribbon means it’s okay to say hello, and “no, thanks” is a complete answer. If someone takes their ribbon off, it means “not now.” WCD takes place in public places, in daylight, and is for adults 18+. Volunteers can be on-site beacons with spare ribbons, and brands and venues can join through the site.

One of the flagship WCD cities will be South Bend, Indiana. On November 21, Notre Dame hosts SMU at Notre Dame Stadium, and ribbons will be available to fans in South Bend on game day.

World Connection Day is a worldwide initiative that will take place three times a year, bringing people together through simple, spontaneous encounters. The November 21 edition coincides with World Hello Day, observed since 1973, and features two official spots in Limassol and South Bend. Looking ahead, the team aims to expand the initiative ahead of its next editions on February 13, 2027, the day before Valentine’s Day, and June 21, 2027, the summer solstice, so that people experiencing loneliness around the world can find a nearby city and find WCD spots nearby.

To take part, take the color test and pick a spot at https://worldconnectionday.com/

Fledge is a dating app designed to help people understand compatibility before they start dating. Going beyond attraction, Fledge uses a research-based approach that considers personality, values, and relationship preferences to identify who may genuinely be a good fit before the first message. The result is fewer, more meaningful matches and a calmer way to date at your own pace, with less pressure, less performance, and more space to be yourself.

Fledge is built by serial entrepreneurs with experience creating dating products used by more than 20 million people, including one of Europe's top-10 dating platforms. Its compatibility model draws on established behavioral science, and the company intends to pursue independent research partnerships. Founded in 2026, Fledge is operated by Fleamily, Inc., a Delaware corporation based in New York. For more information, visit fledge.love

#9766. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9765. What 100,000 Free Characters a Month Covers for a Small Business

"100,000 free characters" sounds generous until you try to picture it. A character is not a word, and nobody thinks in characters when they plan a phone greeting. So here is the arithmetic, done the slow way, for a small business that wants an agent that speaks in a good voice.

Speakvora gives every account 100,000 characters of speech free each calendar month, renewing on the 1st, with no card required. That figure comes from the pricing page and the 21 November 2026 changelog. Everything over it is billed at $3 per 1M characters.

Now divide. Spaces and punctuation count as characters, so a sentence's length is just its length. Take three typical lengths:

The first row is a real sentence I counted; the other two are round lengths. The point is the shape: even at 200 characters a line, the free amount voices about 500 different sentences every month. A bakery or a dental office does not have 500 different things to say in a month. It has a few dozen answers, repeated.

The important word is "different". The free amount is not consumed by calls; it is consumed by new sentences. In Speakvora's speech API, the same text in the same voice returns the stored clip and is not billed or counted (a setting turns that off). In the pay-once agent, a sentence is voiced once and stored by its exact words, then played from disk on every later call. So 10,000 callers hearing "We are open nine to five" cost the same characters as one caller.

This is an illustrative example, not customer data. A shop decides on Friday to announce: "We have 20 percent off all pizzas this weekend only, Saturday and Sunday." I counted it: 73 characters.

The first caller who asks about deals makes the agent produce that sentence. It is new, so it is voiced once, which spends 73 characters. The stored audio is kept, and every later caller who gets that same sentence hears the stored recording: zero further characters. Whether 5 callers ask or 500, the promotion cost 73 characters, or 73 / 1,000,000 x $3 = $0.0002 had it not been inside the free amount. Against 100,000 free characters that is 0.073 percent of the month.

There are two honest caveats. First, "that same sentence" means the same words. If your agent's language model words the offer differently on each call, each variant is a new line and is voiced separately. The agent can learn repeated answers and keep the best wording, which pushes callers toward a single version, but it does not rewrite on its own for you. Second, the first caller may hear the phone provider's built-in voice if the new line is not ready in time; in the agent's greeting path the line is voiced in the background so the next call hears the recording. Voice engines are fast, but "once" still has to happen at some point, and a caller is sometimes the one who triggers it.

Even a restaurant that changes five offers a week, each around 100 characters, spends about 500 characters a week, or roughly 2,000 a month. That is 2 percent of the free amount.

You pass 100,000 characters when you voice a lot of text that does not repeat: personalized messages, long dynamic answers, many languages, or a big library of recordings generated at once. A single 2,900-character page of text is about 3 percent of the month on its own, so reading long documents aloud uses the allowance in a way short phone answers never do. Another way is high volume on the text-to-speech API itself, where every request is new text.

When you do pass it, nothing dramatic happens to the price. Suppose a month of 150,000 characters: the extra 50,000 costs 50,000 / 1,000,000 x $3 = $0.15. A month of 1,000,000 characters costs 900,000 x $3 / 1,000,000 = $2.70 after the free amount. There is no minimum and no monthly fee on the API.

The agent has its own guard, which is not the same thing as the free allowance. New lines it voices in a month are capped at 100,000 characters by default (the guardrail is called talk_chars_per_month, and its fixed ceiling is 200,000), matching the free amount. If that budget is used up, the caller hears the phone provider's voice for that sentence and the agent logs it. Separately, Speakvora's 21 November 2026 changelog says speech made by a pay-once agent is not billed per character, so the cap works as a safety limit on live voicing rather than as a meter. If you run a local voice engine for new lines, those lines use none of your Speakvora characters, at the price of sounding like a different speaker than your recorded lines.

Think of the free amount as a budget for new sentences, not for calls. For most small businesses that means hundreds of distinct lines a month, which is far more than the business actually changes. Count your own lines once: take your twenty most common answers, add their lengths, and you will find the answer is a few thousand characters, not a hundred thousand.

You can check the current allowance and the $3 per 1M price on the Speakvora pricing page, and read how the agent stores and reuses lines on the same site.

The free 100,000 characters per month, no card, $3 per 1M beyond it, and no minimum or monthly fee come from the Speakvora pricing page and changelog (21 November 2026), read 22 November 2026. The agent cap (default 100,000, ceiling 200,000), the provider-voice fallback with logging, local-engine behavior and background voicing of the greeting line come from the agent source files guardrails.py, engine.py and localvoice.py, read the same day. The sentence lengths (36 and 73 characters) were counted by me; the 120 and 200 character rows, the restaurant offers and the 150,000 and 1,000,000 character months are round assumptions used for arithmetic. The 2,900-character page length is from Speakvora's own 2026-11-21 benchmark notes.

#9764. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9763. Your Win Rate Is Wrong Because of the Denominator

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Ask three people in the same company for the win rate and you can get three answers, all calculated correctly, from the same CRM. The numerator is never the argument. Everyone agrees on what a won deal is. The fight is about the denominator: which deals count as a chance you had to win.

That choice can move the number by half. It can also make a quarter look like a disaster when nothing about the sales team changed. Here's a simulated example, the three common formulas, and the one I'd put in front of a leadership team.

I simulated two years of opportunities, about 9,000 of them. The rules never change:

The sales team is exactly as good in every quarter. Any movement in the win rate is bookkeeping.

This is the one most dashboards show. Of the deals that closed this quarter, what share were won?

Two problems. First, the number is low, around 20%, because a third of the denominator is deals that were never real. Disqualifying a bad lead on the first call is good sales behavior, and this formula punishes it.

Second, look at the first quarter of 2026. The win rate halves. Wins are flat at 196. What changed is that the cleanup dumped hundreds of old, quiet deals into the denominator on a single day. If this number goes in a board deck, someone will spend the next month explaining a collapse that never happened.

The obvious fix is to drop the deals that were never qualified.

Better. The number now reflects deals that someone actually worked. But the cleanup quarter is still broken, and there's a quieter problem: in every normal quarter, this formula leaves out the deals nobody closed. They aren't won and they aren't lost, so they don't count. A team that never marks anything lost gets a flattering win rate for free.

That's the real issue with any "closed this quarter" win rate. It measures when someone updated a field, not how deals turned out.

The fix is to stop asking what closed this quarter and ask what happened to the deals created in a quarter. Every deal belongs to exactly one cohort, from the day it's created. It's in the denominator whether anyone ever closes it or not.

The cleanup has disappeared. Each cohort wins about 25 to 27% of its qualified deals, which is the honest answer: about 83% of qualified deals get worked and 32% of those win. Formula 2 said 30% because it quietly ignored the deals that went nowhere.

The cost is that recent cohorts aren't finished. The April 2026 cohort shows 8.6% won, but 72% of its deals are still open. That's not a bad quarter. It's an unfinished one. So always show the still-open column next to a cohort win rate, and don't compare a cohort with its predecessors until it's mostly closed. In this data, that's about two quarters.

Use the cohort win rate as the headline, on qualified deals, for cohorts that are at least 90% closed. It doesn't move when someone cleans up the CRM, and it counts deals that went quiet as what they are: deals you didn't win.

Show the still-open share for recent cohorts, so nobody reads an unfinished cohort as a bad one.

Keep the period win rate as an operational number, not a performance one. It's useful for checking how many deals the team is closing out each week. It's misleading as a measure of how good the team is.

Write the definition down. "Win rate = won deals divided by qualified deals created in the period, measured once the cohort is 90% closed." One sentence settles most of the arguments before they start, and it means sales, marketing, and finance all quote the same number.

Watch for the cleanup. If your company does periodic pipeline cleanups, and most do, any metric built on close dates will spike that quarter. Mark the date on the dashboard or, better, stop building performance metrics on close dates.

Most broken ratios in revenue reporting are broken in the denominator. Win rate, conversion rate, churn rate, attainment: each one hides a choice about who was eligible. Before you trust a ratio, ask what's in the bottom half, and whether something other than performance could change it.

#9762. Certbot Smart Manager: Never Let an SSL Certificate Expire

An expired certificate is the most embarrassing outage in production. No code changed, no deploy happened — yet browsers show a red warning, API clients refuse to connect, and your uptime graph flatlines. I have seen a checkout page go down on a Friday night because nobody owned renewal.

Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days by design. That is a feature, not a bug: short lifetimes force automation. Certbot is the automation. The difference between "we use Certbot" and "certificates never expire" is everything around Certbot — hooks, timers, monitoring, and knowing the failure modes before they hit you at 2 AM.

This is the setup I run in production, and the one I would defend in a DevOps interview.

Certbot speaks ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) to Let's Encrypt. The flow is simple:

There are two challenge types that matter, and picking the wrong one is the most common beginner mistake:

If you need a wildcard, or your server is not publicly reachable on port 80, you need DNS-01. Decide this before you issue your first certificate — switching challenge types later means re-issuing.

The --nginx plugin edits your NGINX config, adds the certificate paths, and sets up the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect. It is the fastest path, but know what it does: it modifies your server config. In production I prefer certonly so my config stays mine.

Note that /etc/letsencrypt/live/ holds symlinks to the latest files in archive/. Never copy the real files elsewhere — always reference the live symlinks, or renewal will silently leave your server on the old certificate.

The credentials file needs a scoped API token (Zone:DNS:Edit for that zone only), and must be locked down:

A leaked DNS API token is a full domain takeover. Treat it like a production secret, because it is one.

Certbot only renews certificates with less than 30 days left. Test renewal before you trust it:

--dry-run uses the Let's Encrypt staging server, so it never counts against rate limits. Run it after every config change. If it fails here, it will fail at 3 AM when the timer fires.

On Debian/Ubuntu, the Certbot package ships a timer that runs twice a day:

That is enough for most servers. But the timer alone does not reload NGINX after renewal. Without a reload, NGINX keeps serving the old certificate from memory until the next restart — the classic "renewal worked but the site still shows expired" bug.

Fix it with a deploy hook, which runs only when a certificate actually renews:

Or make it permanent per-certificate in /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/example.com.conf:

You can also drop scripts in /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/ — every executable there runs after a successful renewal. Pre and post hooks live in renewal-hooks/pre/ and renewal-hooks/post/.

If you use cron instead of the timer (containers, minimal images), use this and nothing cleverer:

Randomize the minute across servers so you don't hammer the ACME API at the same second.

Automation without monitoring is hope. Check what you actually have:

In production, alert on expiry, don't just check it:

Good tools for this: Prometheus blackbox_exporter (probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry), ssl_exporter, or a simple daily cron that emails you. The point is that a human hears about it before the browser warning, not from a customer.

Let's Encrypt rate limits are real, and hitting them during an incident is miserable:

That is why --dry-run (staging) exists, and why you test against staging first when scripting:

If you burn the duplicate limit debugging in production, you wait a week. Debug in staging.

These are the failures I actually see, in order of frequency:

If you are targeting remote DevOps or sysadmin roles, this topic comes up because it reveals how you think about operations:

The answer they want is never "I run certbot once." It is the system around it: automation, hooks, monitoring, and a tested failure path.

Do that, and SSL expiry stops being a class of outage you can have. Certificates are infrastructure: boring, automated, monitored, and never a 2 AM surprise.

Your turn: How do you manage certificates in production — Certbot, a managed load balancer, or an internal CA? What broke for you the first time? Tell me in the comments.

#9761. DeepSeek のピーク・オフピーク料金：実際の節約額

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at tokuse.com

DeepSeek の定価は、通常の平日に2回変わります。同じモデル、同じトークン、同じキャッシュ挙動でも、北京時間の10:00では20:00の2倍のコストがかかることがあります。これはモデル選択の問題である前に、スケジューリングの問題です。

短い答え： ピーク時間帯は平日の北京時間 09:00〜12:00 と 14:00〜18:00 で、中国の法定祝日を除きます。それ以外はすべてピーク料金の半額で課金されます。以下のワークロードでは、同じ2億入力トークンと4,000万出力トークンが、ピークで ¥887.36、オフピークで ¥443.68 になります。ルーティング層を自分で構築したくない場合は、Tokuse アカウントを作成し、両方の DeepSeek モデルに1つの OpenAI 互換エンドポイントを使ってください。ベース URL は https://tokuse.com/v1 です。

DeepSeek は100万トークンあたりの料金を人民元（CNY）で公表しています。現在の Flash と V4 Pro の料金は次のとおりです：

ピーク時間帯は月曜日から金曜日の北京時間 09:00〜12:00 と 14:00〜18:00 です。週末と中国の法定祝日は終日オフピークです。12:00〜14:00 の昼休みもオフピークです。

実測の本番トラフィックではなく、モデル化したワークロードを使ったので、計算は再現できます：

50%の差は時間帯から生まれるものであり、安いモデルや賢いプロンプトによるものではありません。同じワークロードをピーク時間帯の外に移すことが、このモデルで最大の単一レバーです。

オフピークの請求額を支配しているのは出力トークンです。Flash の出力は3,200万トークンで ¥128、Pro の出力は800万トークンで ¥108 です。合計すると、¥443.68 のオフピーク総額のうち ¥236 を占めます。キャッシュヒットは安くなりますが、話の中心ではありません。40%のキャッシュヒット率では、すべての入力トークンにキャッシュミス料金を課した場合と比べて、オフピーク料金で Flash は約 ¥62.72、Pro は約 ¥69.60 節約できます。

これが重要なのは、キャッシュヒット率は過大評価しやすいからです。安定したシステムプロンプトや再利用される RAG プレフィックスは高いヒット率に達することがあります。ロングテールのユーザープロンプトは多くの場合30〜40%程度で、まったくキャッシュにヒットしないワークロードもあります。実測のヒット率が40%ではなく20%なら、節約を約束する前に数字を計算し直してください。

この Python 関数は標準ライブラリだけを使います。現在の時刻がピーク時間帯かどうか、その時刻にトークン構成のコストがいくらになるか、という2つの問いに答えます。

最後の行は 225.28 を出力し、上記の Flash オフピークの数字と一致します。

ピーク判定は中国の法定祝日を認識しません。平日の祝日はピークとして扱われ、コストを過大に見積もります。それが問題になる場合は、祝日カレンダーを追加し、その日付をオフピークとして扱ってください。

価格は執筆時点の公式人民元定価です。変更される可能性があります。キャッシュヒットの前提は最初に実測したい部分です。40%のヒット率はモデル化された入力であり、保証ではありません。モデルの挙動も Flash と Pro で異なるため、コストを節約しても回答品質を変えるルーティングルールは節約とは言えません。

計算は簡単に再現できます。実際のトークン数から始め、DeepSeek コスト計算ツールに通し、ワークロードのうちバッチ部分をピーク時間帯の外に移せるか確認してください。Continue、Cline、LangChain、Cursor、Dify、Open WebUI、OpenAI Node.js SDK の統合ガイドはすべて同じベース URL を使うため、ルーティングの変更はアプリケーションコードの外に留まります。製品の更新情報は変更履歴に記録されています。
