#9760. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9759. Benchmarking AWS Amplify, Lambda, Web Functions, and ECS for Next.js

"Should this run on Amplify, Lambda or ECS?" is usually answered with a feature list. I wanted numbers. So I took one Next.js app, deployed it to four AWS runtimes in the same account and Region, including the new Lambda Web Functions, and measured the things that decide the choice in practice: latency under load, cold starts, CPU speed, real limits, and the monthly bill at four traffic levels.

Lambda and ECS run the exact same container image, and the Web Function runs the same files from a .zip. Amplify Hosting builds the same Git commit. Every command, script, and result is in a public repository, with deploy and cleanup steps:

One app, four runtimes, one DynamoDB table:

The app has a few endpoints, each testing something different:

Every response reports which runtime served it, the CPU architecture, and whether it was the first request of that process (a cold start):

Everything runs in eu-central-1. Lambda and Fargate use arm64 (Graviton) and roughly the same size: Lambda with 1024 MB of memory, and a Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. A Web Function environment has a fixed size of 2 arm64 vCPUs and 2 GB, which you can't change, and Amplify chooses its own compute.

While the setup is running, the only fixed cost is the ECS part: the load balancer, one Fargate task and four public IPv4 addresses, about $1.90 per day. Lambda, Amplify and DynamoDB cost close to nothing at test traffic. Run the cleanup script when you are done.

The app is a normal Next.js app router project. The only special setting is the standalone output, which produces a small self-contained server.js for the container. Amplify builds the app its own way, so the setting is applied only in the Docker build:

The Dockerfile is where Lambda and ECS meet:

--provenance=false keeps a plain single-platform image. By default, buildx adds an attestation manifest and pushes an image index, which Lambda may refuse to use. The script tags each image with the Git commit, so an immutable tag always matches one commit.

Scan on push found one critical CVE on the first push, in zlib from the node:22-alpine base image, not in the app. Base images are rebuilt on a schedule, so security fixes can be days old before they reach the tag you pull. One line in the final stage fixed it:

The next image scanned with zero findings. The compressed image is 88 MB in ECR (233 MB unpacked).

The DynamoDB table is on-demand with one item. Each runtime gets its own IAM role with exactly one permission, dynamodb:GetItem on this table.

A public Function URL now needs both permissions: lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl, and lambda:InvokeFunction limited to calls that come through the URL. I removed the second one to check, and the URL answered with 403 and a helpful message:

A Function URL is free and needs no API Gateway. For production, you would usually put CloudFront in front of it for a custom domain, caching and AWS WAF.

The documented default is 1,000 concurrent executions, but my account had 10. Ten concurrent requests at about 100 ms each is roughly 100 requests per second, and anything above returns 429 Too Many Requests. I requested an increase in Service Quotas (quota code L-B99A9384).

The increase to 1,000 was approved automatically after 2 hours and 20 minutes. Lambda's fast endpoints need far less concurrency than you might expect: at about 40 ms per request, 50 requests per second keep only 2 to 3 environments busy. The CPU endpoint at 50 requests per second peaked at 57 concurrent executions, well over the original limit.

Lambda Web Functions are a new kind of Lambda function for HTTP traffic. Your code is a normal web server that listens on a port, Lambda gives it an HTTPS endpoint, and each execution environment serves many requests at the same time, like a container. It still scales to zero when there is no traffic.

The Next.js standalone server reads HOSTNAME and PORT instead, so the entry file maps one to the other:

To keep the comparison fair, I didn't rebuild the app. The deploy script copies /app out of the same linux/arm64 container image, adds index.js, and deploys that folder:

--include-hidden-files is easy to miss: the Next.js build lives in .next, and without the flag the command leaves hidden folders out of the package. deploy creates the S3 bucket, the function, the first revision and a public endpoint, and waits until the endpoint is active. My first deploy took under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of code and configuration. Changing an environment variable means a new revision, and an endpoint can route traffic to one revision or split it between two, which gives you canary deployments without CodeDeploy.

The pricing model is different from classic Lambda. In eu-central-1 you pay $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time that your code actually uses, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. A request that waits for DynamoDB uses almost no CPU, so it costs very little. But an environment that stays alive costs memory time even between requests: one environment kept alive for a month is about $24 in memory alone.

A Fargate task in a private subnet needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to pull its image, and either costs more than the task itself. For this test, the tasks run in public subnets with a public IP, and the security groups do the protecting:

Two roles, two jobs: the execution role lets ECS pull the image and write logs, and the task role is what your code runs as. The DynamoDB permission goes on the task role only.

Two settings save time on every deploy. The target group health check uses /api/health every 10 seconds with a healthy threshold of 2, so a new task gets traffic in about 20 seconds. The deregistration delay is 10 seconds instead of the default 300, so an old task stops quickly.

One bug from my script is worth sharing: --output text separates a list of subnet IDs with tabs, not spaces. My script turned spaces into commas, so the service request got one "subnet ID" with tabs inside and failed with Subnet ID must match subnet-[0-9a-f]+. Pipe the list through tr '\t' ' '.

Amplify Hosting connects to GitHub with its own GitHub App. It does not use an AWS CodeConnections connection, even if you already have one for CodeBuild or CodePipeline. So the first step is in the console: Create new app, GitHub, choose the repository and the main branch. Amplify detects Next.js and uses the amplify.yml from the repository.

This is the biggest surprise for anyone coming from Lambda or ECS. Amplify passes environment variables to the build, not to the server-side code at runtime. The fix is to write the variables your server code needs into .env.production during the build:

The || true is there because my first build failed without it. Before the variables were set, grep found nothing and exited with code 1, and Amplify stopped the build with "Command failed with exit code 1".

Two more rules: variable names can't start with AWS_, so the app reads APP_REGION instead of AWS_REGION, and secrets should not go into .env.production this way, because they end up in the build artifact.

The server-side code needs AWS credentials to call DynamoDB. Amplify calls this a compute role: an IAM role that amplify.amazonaws.com can assume.

Without a compute role, the page renders but the DynamoDB call fails with a credentials error.

The first response from Amplify answered a question the console doesn't:

AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE is set, so the server code runs on Lambda with 1024 MB, on x64, managed by Amplify. You can't choose the memory size or arm64, and it doesn't count against your account's Lambda concurrency quota.

At 10 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 1,200 requests each):

On light requests, ECS is the fastest, Lambda and the Web Function are close behind with almost the same medians, and Amplify is about 1.5 times slower than Lambda. ECS wins here because nothing sits between the load balancer and a warm Node.js process.

The CPU row is the surprise. One Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU could not keep up with 10 CPU-heavy requests per second: each request needs about 80 to 150 ms of CPU, so the work arrived faster than half a vCPU could do it. Requests queued, the ALB health checks timed out, and ECS replaced the "unhealthy" task in the middle of the test. 8% of requests failed and the median rose to 1.9 seconds. Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify handled the same load without errors, because they add execution environments as the load grows.

The lesson is not that ECS is slow. A fixed-size service needs auto scaling and headroom, and a health check that shares the CPU with the work it checks can turn an overload into a restart.

At 200 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 24,000 requests each):

Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify barely noticed the twentyfold increase: their medians moved by a few milliseconds and no request failed. For the Web Function, I ran the 200 requests per second test twice, because AWS says the first load test on a new Web Function scales conservatively, and the table shows the second run. The two runs were within a few milliseconds of each other. Lambda scaled to 234 concurrent executions in the first seconds of the test, then settled between 50 and 90, with zero throttles.

The single ECS task reached 100% CPU and failed. At 50 requests per second the same task used about 65% CPU on the page endpoint, so one 0.5 vCPU task handles roughly 70 page requests per second before it falls over. For real traffic, you would run at least two tasks with target tracking auto scaling at 50 to 60% CPU.

The 50 requests per second results look like the 10 requests per second ones for Lambda, ECS and Amplify, so I left them in the repository instead of adding another table.

One more number explains why Lambda looks so fast: its billed duration (the CloudWatch Duration metric) was 9 to 16 ms at the median for the light endpoints. Most of the 40 ms that the client sees is the network and the Function URL, not your code.

The CPU endpoint does the same 50,000 hashes everywhere:

Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory: one full vCPU at 1,769 MB. At 1024 MB you get a bit more than half a vCPU, and you pay for the milliseconds you use. A Web Function environment always has 2 vCPUs, and you pay only for the CPU time you use. Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, so a single request can use only one of them, but that one is a full vCPU. Fargate gives you exactly the vCPU you reserve, all the time, whether you use it or not.

Lambda, 10 forced cold starts (the script changes an environment variable before each request):

Amplify, one request after 20 minutes without traffic, 3 times: 1.94 s, 2.00 s and 0.33 s, compared with about 0.16 s for a warm request. All three were served by a new process, so the third one probably landed on an environment that Amplify had already prepared. You can't see or control this, so plan for about 2 seconds on the first request after a quiet period.

Web Function, 5 forced cold starts (each run creates a new revision, which starts new environments):

ECS has no cold start while a task is running, which is what you pay the fixed monthly price for. Scaling out is a different story: in the ECS events, a replacement task registered with the load balancer about 25 seconds after it started, and then needed two 10-second health checks before it got traffic. A new Lambda environment was ready in about one second.

I asked each runtime to wait longer and longer, and to return larger and larger responses:

If your app has report downloads, file exports or slow third-party calls, these limits decide more than any latency number. Classic Lambda can go beyond 6 MB with response streaming, but that needs code changes. With Web Functions, you get it without changes.

Prices are on-demand prices in eu-central-1 from the AWS Price List API, in November 2026, without free tiers:

Web Functions publish their own usage in CloudWatch (EnvironmentCPUTime, EnvironmentActiveTime and ExecutedRequests in the AWS/Lambda/Web namespace), so I could calculate the real bill for my load tests instead of estimating it:

71% of the bill was memory. At 200 requests per second, Lambda ran up to 55 environments, and none of them served more than 2 requests at the same time (the EnvironmentConcurrentRequests maximum). That was the case in both 200 requests per second runs. AWS documents that a new Web Function starts with a conservative per-environment concurrency limit and raises it as it learns, but I didn't see that happen in about 25 minutes of testing. About 30% of the memory time came after the test, while the environments waited about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them.

The same request mix on classic Lambda would cost about $0.15, or $1.04 per million requests. So in my test, Web Functions cost about four times as much. If the per-environment concurrency grows over time, as AWS describes, this gap will shrink, so treat it as the cost of a new function under a load test, not a final verdict.

For the monthly bill, I used the measured durations: 20 ms of Lambda billed time per request (the 9 to 16 ms median, rounded up), and 5 KB per response. Amplify doesn't publish its billed compute time per request; its CloudWatch Latency metric averaged about 100 ms, which includes the CDN, so I show 100 ms as the upper bound and 30 ms as a likely lower bound. ECS uses the measured capacity of about 50 requests per second per task with headroom. For the Web Function, I used 27 ms of CPU per request, at least one environment alive all month (requests arrive more often than every 5 minutes at these levels), and the measured 0.24 environments per request per second at steady load.

The script is in the repository (bench/cost.py), so you can run it with your own durations and response sizes.

The same build runs on classic Lambda, Web Functions and ECS, so this is not a one-way decision. The Web Function in this article is the same /app folder as the container image, plus a 5-line index.js. Starting on Lambda and moving when your traffic or your limits change is a reasonable path.

The script deletes the Amplify app, the ECS service, cluster, load balancer and target group, the Lambda function, the Web Function and its code versions in the shared awscli-lambdaweb-* bucket, the security groups, the ECR repository, the DynamoDB table, the log groups and the IAM roles. Everything it created has the tag project=runtime-benchmark, so you can check in Tag Editor that nothing is left.

The feature lists told me that ECS is "more powerful", Lambda is "serverless" and Amplify is "easy". The measurements told a more useful story. The always-on container was the fastest per request and the first to fail, because one task is a fixed amount of CPU. The three serverless options were a little slower per request but did not care whether traffic was 10 or 200 requests per second. The newest one, Lambda Web Functions, removes most of classic Lambda's limits and was the fastest on CPU, but its memory billing made it the most expensive serverless option in my test. And the limits that matter most for real apps, request timeout and response size, differ by an order of magnitude between them.

If you only take one thing from this article: measure your own app on the runtime you plan to use, before you choose. The repository makes that a few commands, and the cleanup script removes everything when you are done.

#9758. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9757. The Weekend Special Changes Every Week. What Does the Agent Do?

Picture a small restaurant, invented for this example. On Thursday the kitchen decides the weekend special will be braised short ribs. On Friday morning the owner updates the fact in the agent: "Weekend special: braised short ribs with polenta, 24 dollars." On Friday at noon the first caller dials in and asks, "Do you have a special this weekend?"

Everything below is an illustration of how the Speakvora pay-once agent is built to behave, with invented numbers. The arithmetic is mine; the mechanics are from the agent's code.

The agent has recorded lines for the things a restaurant says every day: the greeting, hours, how to book. None of those is the special. So the answer to this caller is a new sentence, written from the owner's facts by the connected AI, say: "This weekend we have braised short ribs with polenta for 24 dollars." I counted that: 66 characters.

The agent checks the store for those exact words and finds nothing. If voicing is allowed, it sends the sentence to the voice engine, stores the audio under a name derived from the exact text, and plays it. In some paths, such as the greeting, a line that is not ready yet is covered by the phone carrier's built-in voice while it is voiced in the background, so the next caller gets the recording. That is the honest first-time cost: a caller may hear a different voice for that sentence, and the agent logs when it falls back.

Cost, in the default cloud mode: 66 characters. At Speakvora's $3 per 1M characters that is 66 / 1,000,000 x $3, about $0.0002. The agent's guard counts those 66 against its monthly budget of 100,000 characters, which is 0.066 percent. (Per Speakvora's changelog of 21 November 2026, speech made by a pay-once agent is not billed per character; the budget is a safety limit, not a meter.)

By Saturday evening, say fifty callers have asked. Caller two asks the same thing, and the AI produces the same sentence. Same words, same key, found in the store: the stored clip plays, with no voicing and no characters spent. The agent refreshes that line's last-used time each time it plays. Callers three to fifty are the same. Total cost for fifty callers: still 66 characters. If you had voiced each reply live, it would be 50 x 66 = 3,300 characters.

Honesty about "the same words": this works only when the AI's sentence is identical. If it produces "This weekend's special is braised short ribs with polenta, 24 dollars" on call seven, that is a different string, so it is a new line, voiced once, costing about 70 characters. The agent has a learning feature that counts repeated customer-facing lines and, at the repeat count the owner sets (default 3), turns a repeated line into a library entry, but it only learns generic lines. Anything with digits is skipped, and this sentence has a 24 in it. So this special would not be learned into the library; it relies on the cache of recently voiced lines, which is exactly what the cache is for. In practice a few wording variants will exist by Sunday, each voiced once. Say five variants: 5 x 70 = 350 characters for the whole weekend.

The next Friday the owner types a new special. Last week's sentences are still in the store, and nobody asks for them. Ordinary voiced lines are kept for 30 days since their last play, so they expire on their own around a month later. Nothing for the owner to clean up, and no stale audio plays, because the key is the words and the new special has new words.

Over a year, with a new special every week and, generously, five wording variants a week at 70 characters, the cost is 52 x 5 x 70 = 18,200 characters. That is 18.2 percent of one month's free allowance, spread across twelve months. Even if the owner announces a second offer every week, you are around 36,000 characters a year.

A busier restaurant changes nothing about the arithmetic, since callers add plays, not characters. What does change it: a long, wordy special description (a 300-character sentence costs four and a half times as much to voice once), a language model that rewords freely (more variants), or a budget that is already used up when the new special arrives, in which case the carrier's voice covers it until the budget renews, and the log says so. If the restaurant would rather never hear the carrier voice on the special, the answer is to keep a spare budget, or to pre-voice the special on Friday morning before the first caller. In the agent's dashboard, lines that are added or edited are voiced right away, with the code noting that a call then plays them instantly.

The practical advice for the owner is short. Put the special in the facts when you decide it, test-call once on Friday so the first real caller does not become the person who triggers the voicing, and let the agent forget last week's.

For more on how the pay-once agent works for restaurants, see speakvora.com; it covers what is included and what the optional support plan costs.

All numbers are for an invented restaurant and are labelled illustrative. Character counts (66, and about 70 for variants) were counted by me. The $3 per 1M characters price and the 100,000-character free allowance are from the Speakvora pricing page, 22 November 2026. The not-billed-per-character statement is from the Speakvora changelog of 21 November 2026. Behavior (cache keyed by exact words, 30-day retention with refresh on use, background voicing with carrier-voice fallback and logging, default 100,000-character budget, learning at a default repeat count of 3 that skips lines with digits, voicing of added or edited lines from the dashboard) is from the agent source files audio.py, engine.py, learned.py, guardrails.py and dashboard.py, read on 22 November 2026.

#9756. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9754. Six Password Reset Vulnerabilities and How to Prevent Them

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

This is an example, not a report from a customer. Imagine a support inbox: someone never asked for a password reset, but they received a "your password was changed" email, and now their login no longer works. Their old password was long and unique. Nobody guessed it.

Nobody needed to. A reset flow is a way into an account without the current password, by design. A valid reset link may let whoever holds it set a new password. Whether that is enough to take the account depends on other controls: a second factor at the reset step, a prompt to re-authenticate, a notification the real owner sees in time, session invalidation after the change, or a token that has already expired or been used.

OWASP calls this functionality "a common source of vulnerabilities" even though it "looks straightforward and easy to implement" (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet). The usual weak points sit at six places in the flow. Run the active tests only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

When someone types an address into "Forgot password", the response should not reveal whether an account exists. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet lists "We just sent you a password reset link" and "This email address doesn't exist in our database" as incorrect responses, and gives the correct one: "If that email address is in our database, we will send you an email to reset your password" (OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet).

The message is the easy part. The Forgot Password Cheat Sheet also asks for responses that "return in a consistent amount of time," for example by sending the email asynchronously instead of exiting early for unknown addresses. A page that answers in a few milliseconds for unknown addresses and noticeably later for real ones tells an attacker the same thing as a different message.

Then rate-limit the endpoint. OWASP recommends per-account rate limiting or a CAPTCHA, because otherwise an attacker can flood a user's inbox. Return the same 429 Too Many Requests whether or not the account exists (RFC 6585, section 4), or the limiter itself becomes an enumeration oracle. Do not lock the account: OWASP notes that a forgotten-password attack should not produce a lockout, because that lets anyone deny access to users whose names they know.

Many frameworks make it easy to build an absolute URL from "the current host". In a reset email, that convenience is the vulnerability. PortSwigger describes password reset poisoning: an attacker submits a reset request for the victim with a Host header pointing at a domain they control, the site sends a genuine token, and the link inside points at the attacker. If the victim clicks it, or a mail scanner fetches it, the token is delivered to the attacker (PortSwigger: Password reset poisoning).

OWASP's instruction is direct: "Don't rely on the Host header while creating the reset URLs." Use one configured HTTPS base URL per environment, and reject host names you do not serve. Treat X-Forwarded-Host the same way: trust it only from your own proxy.

OWASP lists the properties every reset token needs: generated with a cryptographically secure random number generator, long enough to resist brute force, linked to an individual user, invalidated after use, stored securely, and expiring after an appropriate period.

Here is a minimal sketch in Python that follows those properties. It is something to adapt, not a drop-in library.

secrets.token_urlsafe(32) uses Python's module for security tokens, which documents 32 bytes (256 bits) of randomness as sufficient for the typical case (Python docs: secrets). Never use random, timestamps, user IDs or sequential values. Store only a hash, so a leaked database does not contain working links. For a long random token, a fast hash such as SHA-256 is a reasonable choice; slow password hashing is meant for secrets people choose (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet). Issuing a new token should burn older ones for that user. An expired, used or unknown token should produce the same generic error page.

The sketch is single-process and in-memory. In a real application, two requests can redeem the same token at once, so marking it used must be one atomic database operation that succeeds only if it changes exactly one unused, unexpired row.

The token sits in a URL, and URLs travel.

OWASP asks reset pages to send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. When no policy is set, browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, which sends only the origin on cross-origin requests (MDN: Referrer-Policy). A missing header is not proof that the token leaks to third parties in current browsers. It is a missing layer: the default still sends the full URL on same-origin requests, and a looser policy elsewhere on the site would apply.

Analytics, chat widgets and session-replay tools on the reset page can read location.href. The cleanest pattern is a reset page with no third-party scripts. Mail scanners can also open the link before the user does. If a GET burns the single-use token, the real user may find it "already used". Show the form on GET, and consume the token only on POST.

If an attacker already had a session, a new password alone does not remove them. OWASP recommends invalidating existing sessions, or asking the user whether to do so, and advises against signing the user in automatically after the reset. The Session Management Cheat Sheet lists a completed password change among the events that should require reauthentication (OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet).

Send a notification that the password was changed, without the password in it, as OWASP recommends. In the example above, that email is what turned a silent change into a support ticket. Include a way to report "this wasn't me" that does not depend on the account's current password.

Use two test accounts you control, and staging where possible. We have not run the commands below against a live site.

Submit the form for a real test address and for an address that does not exist, and compare status, visible message, size and timing. You want the same status and message for both. A "no such user" error is a leak. Small size differences can come from a CSRF token; timing needs many requests before it means anything.

In staging, send the same request with a foreign Host (and again with X-Forwarded-Host) and read the email that arrives. If the link points at the foreign host, that header is being trusted. A 404 or 421 from the proxy only shows that this request was refused; read the link-building code as well.

With a test account, reuse a spent link, use the older of two links, wait past expiry, and open the page with GET before submitting the form. The last check shows whether a GET burns the token. Look at the reset page for Referrer-Policy and third-party scripts. After a reset, a second browser that was already signed in should be signed out or asked to authenticate again.

If every step behaved as intended for these test accounts, this flow did what you asked when you tested it. Other recovery paths, and the difference between staging and production, still need their own review.

We are the HackerMe team, and we build a free scanner for public pages and headers. It cannot read reset emails or token storage.

#9753. DeepSeek 피크 vs 비피크 가격: 실제 절감 효과

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at tokuse.com

DeepSeek의 정가는 평일 하루에 두 번 바뀝니다. 같은 모델, 같은 토큰, 같은 캐시 동작이라도 베이징 시간 10:00에는 20:00보다 두 배의 비용이 들 수 있습니다. 이것은 모델 선택 문제이기 전에 일정 문제입니다.

간단한 답: 피크 시간대는 평일 베이징 시간 09:00–12:00 및 14:00–18:00이며, 중국 법정 공휴일은 제외됩니다. 그 외 모든 시간은 피크 요율의 절반으로 청구됩니다. 아래 워크로드에서 동일한 2억 입력 토큰과 4,000만 출력 토큰은 피크에 ¥887.36, 비피크에 ¥443.68입니다. 라우팅 계층을 직접 구축하고 싶지 않다면 Tokuse 계정을 만들고 두 DeepSeek 모델 모두에 하나의 OpenAI 호환 엔드포인트를 사용하세요. 기본 URL은 https://tokuse.com/v1입니다.

DeepSeek는 100만 토큰당 가격을 위안화(CNY)로 공시합니다. 현재 Flash와 V4 Pro 가격은 다음과 같습니다:

피크 시간대는 월요일부터 금요일까지 베이징 시간 09:00–12:00 및 14:00–18:00입니다. 주말과 중국 법정 공휴일은 종일 비피크입니다. 12:00–14:00 점심시간도 비피크입니다.

실측 프로덕션 트래픽이 아니라 모델링한 워크로드를 사용했으므로 계산을 재현할 수 있습니다:

50% 차이는 더 저렴한 모델이나 영리한 프롬프트가 아니라 시계에서 나옵니다. 동일한 워크로드를 피크 시간대 밖으로 옮기는 것이 이 모델에서 가장 큰 단일 레버입니다.

비피크 청구서를 지배하는 것은 출력 토큰입니다. Flash 출력은 3,200만 토큰에 ¥128이고, Pro 출력은 800만 토큰에 ¥108입니다. 합치면 ¥443.68 비피크 총액 중 ¥236입니다. 캐시 적중은 더 저렴하지만 주된 이야기는 아닙니다. 캐시 적중률 40%에서 모든 입력 토큰에 캐시 미적중 요율을 적용할 때보다 비피크 요율로 Flash는 약 ¥62.72, Pro는 약 ¥69.60을 절약합니다.

이는 캐시 적중률을 과대평가하기 쉽기 때문에 중요합니다. 안정적인 시스템 프롬프트와 재사용되는 RAG 접두사는 높은 적중률에 도달할 수 있습니다. 롱테일 사용자 프롬프트는 흔히 30–40% 수준이며, 일부 워크로드는 캐시에 전혀 적중하지 않습니다. 측정된 적중률이 40%가 아니라 20%라면 절감을 약속하기 전에 숫자를 다시 계산하세요.

네 가지 규칙을 유지하겠습니다. 어느 것도 새 모델을 필요로 하지 않습니다.

이 Python 함수는 표준 라이브러리만 사용합니다. 현재 시간이 피크 시간대인지, 그 시간에 토큰 구성 비용이 얼마인지 두 가지 질문에 답합니다.

마지막 줄은 225.28을 출력하며, 위의 Flash 비피크 수치와 일치합니다.

피크 판정은 중국 법정 공휴일을 알지 못합니다. 평일 공휴일은 피크로 처리되어 비용을 과대 산정합니다. 이것이 중요하다면 공휴일 캘린더를 추가하고 해당 날짜를 비피크로 처리하세요.

가격은 작성 시점의 공식 위안화 정가입니다. 바뀔 수 있습니다. 캐시 적중 가정은 제가 가장 먼저 측정하고 싶은 부분입니다. 40% 적중률은 모델링된 입력이며 보장이 아닙니다. 모델 동작도 Flash와 Pro가 다르므로, 비용은 줄지만 답변 품질을 바꾸는 라우팅 규칙은 절감이 아닙니다.

계산은 쉽게 재현할 수 있습니다. 실제 토큰 수에서 시작해 DeepSeek 비용 계산기에 넣고, 워크로드의 배치 부분을 피크 시간대 밖으로 옮길 수 있는지 확인하세요. Continue, Cline, LangChain, Cursor, Dify, Open WebUI, OpenAI Node.js SDK 통합 가이드는 모두 동일한 기본 URL을 사용하므로 라우팅 변경은 애플리케이션 코드 밖에 머뭅니다. 제품 업데이트는 변경 로그에 기록됩니다.

#9752. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

  

 The marketing industry is turning to artificial intelligence (AI) as a way to save time and execute smarter, more personalized campaigns. 61% of marketers say AI software is the most important aspect of their data strategy.

  If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

1. Jasper Ai(Formerly known as Jarvis)


Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Key Features

  •  It's trusted by 50,000+ marketers for creating engaging marketing campaigns, ad copy, blog posts, and articles within minutes which would traditionally take hours or days. Special Features:
  • Blog posts have been optimized for search engines and rank high on Google and other search engines. This is a huge plus for online businesses that want to generate traffic to their website through content marketing.
  • 99.9% Original Content and guarantees that all content it generates will be original, so businesses can focus on their online reputation rather than worrying about penalties from Google for duplicate content.
  • Long-Form Article Writing – Jasper.ai is also useful for long-form writing, allowing users to create articles of up to 10,000 words without any difficulty. This is ideal for businesses that want to produce in-depth content that will capture their audience’s attention.

2. Personalize

 Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Key Features

  • Identifies  top three interests based on metrics like time on page, recency, and frequency of each contact
  • Works with every ESP and CRM
  • Easy to get up and running in days
  • Enterprise-grade technology at a low cost for SMBs

3. Seventh Sense

  Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers 

Key Features 

  • AI determines the best send-time and email frequency for each contact
  • Connects with HubSpot and Marketo

4. Phrasee

  Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

Key Features 

  • Instantly generates millions of human-sounding, brand-compliant copy variants
  • Creates tailored language models for every customer
  • Learns what your audience responds to and rebuilds the prediction model every time

5. Hubspot Seo

  HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

Key Features 

  • Helps you discover and rank topics that people are searching for
  • Provides suggestions for your topic clusters and related subjects
  • Integrates with all other HubSpot content tools to help you create a well-rounded content strategy

 6. Evolve AI

  When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Key Features 

  • Figures out which content provides the best performance
  • Lets you test multiple ideas in a single experiment instead of having to perform many individual tests over a long period
  • Lets you try all your ideas across multiple pages for full-funnel optimization
  • Offers visual and code editors

7. Acrolinx

  Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

Key features

  • Reviews and scores existing content to ensure it meets your brand guidelines
  • Finds opportunities to improve your content and use automation to shorten your editorial process.
  • Integrates with more than 50 tools and platforms, including Google Docs, Microsoft Word, WordPress, and most web browsers.

8. MarketMuse 

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Key features:

  • The built-in editor shows how in-depth your topic is covered and what needs improvement
  • Finds gaps and opportunities for new content creation, prioritized by their probable impact and your chance of ranking

9. Copilot

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Key features: 

  • Integrate Facebook Messenger directly with your website, including chat history and recent interactions for a fluid customer service experience 
  • Run drip messenger campaigns to keep customers engaged with your brand
  • Send abandoned carts, out-of-stock, restock, preorder, order status, and shipment notifications to contacts 
  • Send branded images, promotional content, or coupon codes to those who opt in
  • Collect post-purchase feedback, reviews, and customer insight
  • Demonstrate social proof on your website with a widget, or push automatic Facebook posts sharing recent purchases
  • Display a promotional banner on your website to capture contacts instantly
Also Read: Top 10 AI Content Generator & Writer Tools in 2022

10. Yotpo

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Key features:

  • Makes it easy for shoppers to filter reviews and find the exact information they’re looking for
  • Analyzes customer feedback and sentiments to help you improve your products
  • Integrates with most leading eCommerce platforms, including BigCommerce, Magento, and Shopify.

11. Albert AI

  Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

  Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

Key features:

  • Breaks down large amounts of data to help you customize campaigns
  • Plugs into your marketing technology stack and can be used across diverse media outlets, including email, content, paid media, and mobile

Final Saying

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9751. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

#9750. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9749. */5 does not start five minutes from now

*/5 does not mean “five minutes after you save the crontab.” The line */5 * * * * is locked to the clock. It runs at minute 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, and 55 of every hour. Install it at 10:03 and the next run is 10:05, then 10:10. The schedule does not remember when you edited the file.

Build the five fields in the cron expression generator. The page does not install the job. Copy the expression into the crontab on the machine that will run it.

Each of those includes minute 0. 5-59/5 * * * * is different: the range starts at 5, so minute 0 is skipped. Use that only when you really want to skip the top of the hour.

To wait five minutes from an arbitrary moment, sleep inside a process, or use a queue’s delay. Cron will still wake up on minutes 0, 5, 10, and the rest. Five-field cron has no seconds field. The daemon starts once when the matching minute begins.

Do not paste a Quartz or EventBridge line into a five-field crontab. Call the program by its absolute path. Cron’s PATH is often short.

Guide: https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-every-5-minutes
